evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Ancient Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: character evolution; stage labels and received component account
evidence.text: The entry lists oracle-bone, bronze (including inscription collection no. 04293), Chu manuscript, small-seal, and Shuowen forms. It describes 名 as upper 夕 and lower 口, and gives both a semantic role in the traditional story of calling out one’s name at night. This records a received interpretation; it does not independently establish the original motivation.
evidence.title: 漢字「名」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 夕 and 名 component analyses; cited attestations
evidence.text: The entry says 夕’s basic sense is sunset/moonrise, with some uses extending to night. It repeats the Shuowen account for 名. Cited uses include an oracle-bone place-name token 《乙》3290; Western Zhou bronze 名 as ‘name/designate’ on the 少虡 sword; 鑄公華鐘 名 read as 銘 ‘inscription’; and Warring States manuscript uses for name/designation in 清華簡《楚居》簡9, 《保訓》簡6, 郭店簡《老子甲》簡18 and 《太一生水》簡10. These attestations document uses but do not establish a linear semantic chronology.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 夕 (includes 名 entry)

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry reports that 夕 and 月 both used a moon-like form before graphic differentiation; it says a dot later distinguished 月 from 夕. It cites oracle-bone examples with 夕 meaning evening, including ‘今夕雨’ and ‘王夕出’. Its note identifies the evening/moonrise interval as the basic sense and says 夕 can sometimes extend to night.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫: 夕

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: Shuowen account; listed meanings; historical dictionary witnesses
evidence.text: The entry records the Shuowen explanation of 名 as self-designation, from 口 and 夕, with 夕 glossed as darkness. It lists meanings including personal designation, naming, names of things, written characters, conceptual names, status, reputation, category, and classifier uses. It cites historical dictionary sources including Shuowen, Yupian, Guangyun and Jiyun; the page does not itself date the first occurrence of each sense.
evidence.title: [A00508] 名 - Ministry of Education 《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》2024

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The page prints the Shuowen form and analysis 从口从夕, and gives modern Taiwan Mandarin míng. It also supplies cited classical examples for senses such as personal name, naming, thing-name, and fame, but the order of listed senses is not treated as chronology.
evidence.title: [A00508] 名 - Ministry of Education 《Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants》2024

gaps: The retrieved material repeats the traditional semantic 夕 + 口 explanation but does not independently demonstrate that it was the original motivation of the graph.

An alternative reported in the dossier—that 夕 served as a phonetic indicator, possibly associated with a graph later written 明—remains without a directly inspected primary paleographic defense here; it is not adopted as established analysis.
The earliest reported oracle-bone use is a place-name token, not an unambiguous common-noun ‘name’; the cited database page does not resolve its date or semantics further.

Attestations show place-name, naming, inscription, and Warring States name/designation uses, but they do not establish first dates for ‘personal name’, ‘reputation’, ‘rank’, classifier or other extensions, nor a continuous semantic path. Dictionary gloss order is not chronology.
No independent original-object/name borrowing analysis was needed for this graph account; no borrowing claim is advanced.

Modern readings and historical reconstruction comparisons are not reasserted as sound-component evidence. The local Mandarin rows for 名, 夕, and 口 lack verified official Unicode character-page click-throughs in this invocation; Unihan is current metadata and would not itself establish an ancient sound relationship.
The official Xiaoxuetang CC0 terms were inspected, but its character-specific query did not load through the web tool, so no source-label-specific glyph could be selected.

Commons vector glyphs are modern redrawings rather than artifact photographs. Their exact original-file pages were verified, but browser fetches of both SVG assets failed with cache misses; pixels were not visually inspected.
